entities.name: Aristonous of Pella
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aristonous of Pella (born c. 350 BCE in Pella, died 314 BCE in Amphipolis) was a distinguished Macedonian officer and administrator whose career spanned the final years of Alexander the Great's empire and the tumultuous early phase of the Wars of the Diadochi. As one of Alexander's seven Somatophylakes (bodyguards) and later a general, Aristonous represented the elite cadre of loyal lieutenants crucial to the Macedonian war machine and imperial administration. His unwavering adherence to Alexander's royal family, particularly Roxane and Alexander IV, ultimately sealed his fate amidst the ruthless power struggles that fragmented the Hellenistic world.

His military service included significant participation in Alexander's campaigns, notably the Indian expedition where he distinguished himself, and later at the Susa weddings in 324 BCE, where he was honored with a golden crown for valor. Following Alexander's death in 323 BCE, Aristonous became a key player in the ensuing conflicts. He initially supported Perdiccas and later Eumenes of Cardia, steadfastly defending the Argead dynasty's claim against the ambitions of the emerging Hellenistic monarchs. His administrative capabilities were evident during his tenure as governor of Amphipolis, a strategically vital Macedonian city, where he maintained order and control amidst widespread instability.

Aristonous's ultimate downfall in 314 BCE, when he was executed by Cassander after being handed over by Antigonus I Monophthalmus, vividly illustrates the brutal nature of the Diadochi Wars. His death marked another step in the systematic elimination of figures loyal to the legitimate Argead line, thereby paving the way for the establishment of new dynastic monarchies. His fate serves as a poignant example of how personal loyalty, once a virtue in Alexander's court, became a fatal liability in the cutthroat political landscape that followed, where alliances were fluid and power was seized through force and betrayal.
